prompt: Hypothetical. Closes for the last five days were Rs 100, Rs 102, Rs 104, Rs 106 and Rs 108. What is the simple average of the five closes?
Hypothetical. Three indicators on one chart all use the same daily closes. They all say the price is rising. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The three indicators are three independent proofs that the price will keep rising
The three indicators may be counting the same input in three ways, so they are not three separate pieces of evidence
Three agreeing indicators prove the data is correct
Three agreeing indicators make the stop unnecessary

explanations.a: Indicators built from the same closes often share one input. Agreement may reflect that shared input, not three separate tests.
explanations.c: Agreement says nothing about whether the data is correct. It only says the readings match.
explanations.d: Stops and position size still apply even when indicators agree. Agreement is not a risk limit.

prompt: Hypothetical. A reader has a trade that lost money. The reader changes the average period from 20 days to 14 days, then to 9 days, until the old trade looks profitable on the chart. The reader says, 'Now I know the right setting.' Which response fits the book's rules?

options.text: Agree. A setting that makes the old trade look profitable is the right setting
Stop. Changing the period after seeing the result is overfitting. Record every setting tried, and fix the periods before any new test
Keep the 9-day setting, because shorter averages are always better
Ignore the chart, because one trade cannot show anything

explanations.a: A setting picked because it makes one past trade look good has been fitted to the past. It has not been tested on new data.
explanations.c: No period is always better. A shorter average reacts faster but does not prove a better result.
explanations.d: One trade shows little. The mistake here is the changing setting, which can fit almost any past trade.

prompt: Hypothetical. Closes Rs 100 and Rs 110 on day 1 and day 2, with a 2-day average of Rs 105. Using only these numbers, how far above the average is the day 2 close, in rupees?
solution: The 2-day average on day 2 is (100 + 110) / 2 = Rs 105, as given. The day 2 close is Rs 110. Difference = 110 - 105 = Rs 5.

prompt: Read this statement. Which part holds the root mistake? 'The 20-day average, the MACD and the RSI all say up, so I have three independent confirmations. Three confirmations make the trade much safer.'

options.text: The 20-day average, the MACD and the RSI all say up
So I have three independent confirmations
Three confirmations make the trade much safer

explanations.a: This part reads the indicators as stated. The mistake is in calling them independent, which needs their inputs to be different.
explanations.c: This part is also wrong, but only because it rests on the claim of three independent confirmations. The root mistake is in the second part. Agreement is not a safety measure, and a stop and size are still needed.

prompt: A tie-break rule is written before a test. Which rule is the best fit for this book?

options.text: Trade whichever indicator gave the best result last week
Use two named indicators with fixed periods. If they disagree, allow no trade that day
Use every indicator on the chart and follow the majority
Change the periods each day until the two indicators agree

explanations.a: Choosing the indicator that did best last week fits the past. It is a setting picked after seeing results.
explanations.c: A majority count treats redundant indicators as separate votes. It also uses more settings, which makes fitting easier.
explanations.d: Changing periods until two indicators agree is the self-deception this chapter warns about.

prompt: Hypothetical. A reader says: 'When indicators disagree, the data must be wrong. I will check the data until the indicators match.' Which response fits the book's rules?

options.text: Agree. Disagreement is a sign of bad data
Disagreement is normal. Check the data for errors, but decide in advance what the rule does when indicators disagree
Pick the indicator that agrees with the trader's view

explanations.a: Indicators often disagree for real reasons, such as different periods or different inputs. Disagreement alone does not show bad data.
explanations.c: Picking the indicator that agrees with the view is hindsight. The rule must be written before the data is read.
explanations.d: Indicators can describe the past. The point is to use them with a fixed rule and to avoid treating them as forecasts.
